title: Quantum Magic in High Energy Collision
authors: Ying-Ying Li, Ian Low, Yi-Lin Wang, Zhewei Yin
abstract: Quantum magic, or nonstabilizerness, is a quantum resource associated with computational advantage in quantum systems. In high energy collisions, Quantum Electrodynamics (QED) is inefficient at generating magic   while the weak mixing angle, a fundamental constant of nature, sits near a value that minimizes magic production in charged-lepton scattering. These observations were made in the laboratory (lab) basis, in which spin is projected along the incoming beam axis. An alternative choice is the helicity basis, in which spin is projected along the direction of motion of each particle. The transformation between these two bases is, in general, not a Clifford operation and therefore can change the amount of magic. We present a detailed study of magic production in both bases for QED and electroweak processes, and compare these results with the basis-invariant non-local magic. In the ultra-relativistic limit, magic production is generally smaller in the helicity basis due to helicity selection rules, while the lab basis generally yields less magic in the non-relativistic regime. We provide circuit realizations of the ultra-relativistic Bhabha amplitudes using linear combinations of unitaries and show that the lab basis construction contains a larger $T$-gate count at generic scattering angles. Interestingly, in both bases the physical weak mixing angle lies close to the value that minimizes magic production.
summary: This paper investigates 'quantum magic,' a quantum resource, by applying it to high-energy particle collisions in QED and electroweak processes. It compares the amount of magic generated when spin is projected using two different reference frames: the lab basis and the helicity basis. The findings highlight basis dependence in quantum resources and confirm the robustness of the weak mixing angle measurement across these different physical bases.
main_problem: The paper quantifies 'quantum magic' (non-stabilizerness) as a resource, extending its application from quantum computing to fundamental high-energy physics processes.
main_result: Magic production is generally smaller in the helicity basis in the ultra-relativistic limit, while the physical weak mixing angle remains close to the magic-minimizing value in both the lab and helicity bases.
method: The authors calculate the resource using the second-order Stabilizer Rényi entropy ($M_2$) and compare its value when spin is projected along the incoming beam axis (lab basis) versus the direction of particle motion (helicity basis).
model_or_system: The study models high energy collisions involving Quantum Electrodynamics (QED) and electroweak processes (charged-lepton scattering) using spin-1/2 fermions (qubits).
key_observables: Quantum Magic ($M_2$), basis dependence of magic, and the value of the weak mixing angle ($\sin^2 	heta_W$).
important_parameters: Ultra-relativistic limit, non-relativistic regime, and the weak mixing angle ($\sin^2 	heta_W$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the applicability of the $M_2$ measure and compares results derived from the lab basis versus the helicity basis.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the difference between the helicity and lab bases for spin projection. Figure 2 plots the non-zero angular distributions of $M_2$ generated by rotations.
paper_structure: The paper systematically compares magic production in the lab and helicity bases for QED and electroweak scattering processes, analyzing both ultra-relativistic and non-relativistic limits, and discussing circuit realizations.
why_interesting: The concept of basis-dependent quantum resources like 'magic' provides a novel lens through which to view fundamental symmetries and physical constants in particle physics, potentially linking quantum information theory to high-energy phenomenology.
